[p. 2] … (23) Accent — / (in the examples below the neutral accent has been left unmarked): pīr 'saint' / pī/r 'wife's natal home'; gorī 'fair-skinned woman' / go/rī 'cowherd'; paur 'last year' / pau/r 'watch of the day' [p. 6] … For the suprasegmental phoneme 'neutral accent' there is no sign in the script, which is reasonable. new_statements.rule_in_words: Bahl treats accent (svarāghāt) as a suprasegmental phoneme with two values: an unmarked 'neutral' accent and a lexically contrastive 'rising' accent attached to a specific syllable; the rising accent distinguishes word pairs that are segmentally identical (historically the syllable before a lost /h/: pīhar > pī/r, sasur > so/rī, gvālā > go/rī, prahar > pau/r, syāhī > sa/ī). He gives no rule for where the neutral accent (default word stress) falls, and no statement that stress is predictable; the description is of a lexical pitch/rising accent, not of stress placement.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; only that the rising accent is frequently left unwritten in written Modern Rajasthani.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms: minimal pairs of isolated words (pp. 6-7). Variety: standard Marwari of Jodhpur/Bikaner, phonology based on the Mathaniya and Rotunda dialects (preface p. ii). Read from the scan images (no text; my Hindi scanned checked against the page scan); the term svarāghāt is the standard Hindi term for accent/stress, and 'ārohī' (rising) marks it as a pitch contour — the same phenomenon Gusain calls 'tones' and Allen 1957 'aspiration/murmur'.
new_statements.identity_note: Bahl 1980 describes 'Modern Rajasthani' = the standard form current in Jodhpur and Bikaner (Marwari proper); the phonology chapter is based on the Mathaniya and 'Rotunda' dialects of Jodhpur district and, per the preface, applies to the other Jodhpur/Bikaner forms. This is marw1260 (Standard Marwari), the same variety Mukherjee 2011 (Jodhpur informants) describes. Note the statement is about a lexically contrastive rising accent (the well-known Rajasthani 'tone' from lost /h/), not a default word-stress placement rule.

new_statements.quote: Another interesting problem in the analysis of the Mārwāṛī vowels is that of pitch or tone. Asopa [1896:27-28] noticed that in some words, the vowels received a special 'acute' accent (udātt). [...] Bahl [1972, 1980] does describe this 'pitch' (svarāghāt) and treats it as another suprasegmental phoneme. I found that this accent is phonetically a high-falling tone, and it may occur on any vowel. [...] this tone is particularly significant in the verbal system, where, placed on the last vowel of the verb stem, it forms the "inferred future" tense. As will be shown later, this tone seems to result from loss of an [h] in the following syllable.

Quote, locator, reading and relation are identical to index 1 and were verified there against th…
new_statements.relation_note: Same text as index 1: confirms the catalog's 'tonal' kind (Bahl 1980 svaraghat) with independent field data; adds phonetic contour (high-falling; Bahl's label is arohi 'rising'), distribution (any vowel), diachronic source (loss of following [h] < /s/) and the grammatical inferred-future tone on the stem-final syllable; no word-stress placement statement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No word-stress placement rule is given anywhere in the dissertation (1.2 'Marwari Phonology', pp. 23-39, is an avowedly informal overview: 'my analysis.. did not include any attempt at true phonological investigation', p. 23; the phrase 'after a stressed vowel' is used incidentally on pp. 30 and 38 without saying where stress falls). What Magier does state is a phonemic suprasegmental TONE: Bahl's svaraghat is 'phonetically a high-falling tone' that 'may occur on any vowel', marked with an apostrophe over the vowel; it lengthens short vowels phonetically; it is phonemic with minimal pairs (p. 38, citing Asopa 1896:28-9, Bahl 1972:16, 1980:6); diachronically it arises from loss of [h] (itself often < /s/) in the following syllable, falling 'on the vowel in the syllable immediately preceding the elided consonant' (p. 38); grammatically, a high-falling tone on the last syllable of the verb stem plus -ī forms the 'inferred future' (3.2.1.9, pp. 128-129, 131: 'the regular spoken form of the inferred future is with the falling tone'). He marks the tone only where clearly distinctive.
new_statements.exceptions: Tone 'does not always arise when /s/ or /h/ are elided. (Thus [lāpī], not *[lā'pī] for /lāpsī/)' (p. 38); Magier marks the tone 'only where it is clearly distinctive, as in the case of its use as a grammatical marker of the inferred future tense' (p. 38); the phonemic status of the tone is called 'somewhat problematic' (p. 129).
new_statements.identity_note: Magier describes the spoken Marwari of Jodhpur city and district (fieldwork in Jodhpur and the village of Borunda, Rupayan Sansthan; informant/assistant Manohar Lalas), western Rajasthan; he notes sub-dialect variation (e.g. Pushkarna Brahmin speech of Jodhpur) and contrasts his data with Bahl's Marwar Mathania informant.

sources.note: Ch. 1 §1.2.3 (p. 2) lists suprasegmental phonemes: nasality, and svarāghāt (accent) with two values, nirapekṣ 'neutral' (unmarked) vs ārohī 'rising' (marked after the syllable); (23) p. 6 gives minimal pairs for the rising accent (pīr 'saint' vs pī/r 'wife's natal home', gorī vs go/rī 'cowherd', paur vs pau/r 'watch of the day'); p. 7: neutral accent has no written sign, rising accent is marked on the syllable that bears it and is often left unwritten. No rule for where the neutral accent falls; no stress-placement rule.
